concept.title: RootishArrayStack 的浪费空间界
concept.core_question: 为什么 RootishArrayStack 只浪费 O(sqrt(n)) 个数组槽位？
concept.summary: 收缩规则保证最多两个末尾块不满，而块数 r=O(sqrt(n))，所以未用槽位与块目录开销均为 O(sqrt(n))。
concept.definition: 若 RootishArrayStack 存有 n 个元素和 r 个块，收缩不变量给出 $(r-2)(r-1)/2\le n$，从而 $r\le(3+\sqrt{8n+1})/2=O(\sqrt n)$。仅最后两个块可能不满，其总长度至多 2r-1；保存 r 个块引用也需 O(r) 空间，因此总浪费空间为 $O(\sqrt n)$。

relations.description: 理解《RootishArrayStack 的浪费空间界》是继续学习目标知识点的直接基础。

rookie_explanation.analogy: 逐层变长的书架中，只有最后一两层可能空着较多位置；层数只按藏书量的平方根增长，所以空位也受平方根级别限制。
rookie_explanation.boundary: 类比表达渐近上界，不给出具体 n 下的精确内存字节数或对象头开销。

related_concepts.title: RootishArrayStack 的块增长与收缩
related_concepts.core_question: RootishArrayStack 何时增加或删除数组块？
related_concepts.summary: 容量不足时追加长度 r+1 的块，空块超过一个时删除尾部多余块，并保持最多两个块未完全装满。
related_concepts.definition: 若 r 个块的总容量 $r(r+1)/2$ 小于 n+1，grow 追加一个长度为 r+1 的数组块。删除后，shrink 在移除倒数第二块仍能容纳 n 个元素时持续删除尾块，从而只保留必要块和至多一个额外空块。grow 与 shrink 本身不复制已有元素。

related_concepts.title: RootishArrayStack 的时间与空间复杂度
related_concepts.core_question: RootishArrayStack 在随机访问、更新和额外空间之间做了怎样的权衡？
related_concepts.summary: 它保留 O(1) 随机访问和 O(1+n-i) 按位更新，同时把浪费空间降为 O(sqrt(n))。
related_concepts.definition: RootishArrayStack 的 get 与 set 为 $O(1)$，忽略 grow 与 shrink 时，add(i,x) 与 remove(i) 为 $O(1+n-i)$。从空结构开始的 m 次更新中，块增长和收缩的总成本为 $O(m)$；在任意时刻，未使用槽位和块目录造成的额外空间为 $O(\sqrt n)$。

source_records.content: \seclabel{rootishspaceusage} Next, we analyze the amount of extra space used by a RootishArrayStack. In particular, we want to count any space used by a RootishArrayStack that is not an array element currently used to hold a list element. We call all such space \emph{wasted space}. \index{wasted space} The \ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathrm{remove}(\ensuremath{\mathit{i}})}} operation ensures that a RootishArrayStack never has more than two blocks that are not completely full. The number of blocks, \ensuremath{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathit{r}}}}, used by a RootishArrayStack that stores \ensuremath{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathit{n}}}} elements therefore satisfies
Again, using the quadratic equation on this gives

The last two blocks have sizes \ensuremath{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathit{r}}}} and \ensuremath{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathit{r}}-1}}, so the space wasted by these two blocks is at most $2\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathit{r}}}}-1 = O(\sqrt{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathit{n}}}}})$. If we store the blocks in (for example) an ArrayStack, then the amount of space wasted by the List that stores those \ensuremath{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathit{r}}}} blocks is also $O(\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathit{r}}}})=O(\sqrt{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathit{n}}}}})$. The other space needed for storing \ensuremath{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathit{n}}}} and other accounting information is $O(1)$. Therefore, the total amount of wasted space in a RootishArrayStack is $O(\sqrt{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathit{n}}}}})$. Next, we argue that this space usage is optimal for any data structure that starts out empty and can support the addition of one item at a time. More precisely, we will show that, at some point during the addition of \ensuremath{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathit{n}}}} items, the data structure is wasting at least in $\sqrt{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathit{n}}}}}$ space (though it may be only wasted for a moment). Suppose we start with an empty data structure and we add \ensuremath{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathit{n}}}} items one at a time. At the end of this process, all \ensuremath{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathit{n}}}} items are stored in the structure and distributed among a collection of \ensuremath{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathit{r}}}} memory blocks. If $\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathit{r}}}}\ge \sqrt{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathit{n}}}}}$, then the data structure must be using \ensuremath{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathit{r}}}} pointers (or references) to keep track of these \ensuremath{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathit{r}}}} blocks, and these pointers are wasted space. On the other hand, if $\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathit{r}}}} < \sqrt{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathit{n}}}}}$ then, by the pigeonhole principle, some block must have size at least $\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathit{n}}}}/\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathit{r}}}} > \sqrt{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathit{n}}}}}$. Consider the moment at which this block was first allocated. Immediately after it was allocated, this block was empty, and was therefore wasting $\sqrt{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathit{n}}}}}$ space. Therefore, at some point in time during the insertion of \ensuremath{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathit{n}}}} elements, the data structure was wasting $\sqrt{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathit{n}}}}}$ space.
